benefits: See the lifetime cost of a 1% fee in real money - it shocks most people.

faqs.a: The expense ratio is the annual percentage a fund charges on your assets: 1.5% means $150 per year on every $10,000 invested, taken quietly from returns. Index funds often charge 0.03-0.20%; actively managed funds often charge 0.75-2%.

Because of compounding: the fee is taken every year, and each year's fee also misses out on all future growth. A 1.5% fee over 30 years at 7% return does not cost 45% of one year's gains - it costs about 35% of your final balance.
faqs.q: Why do small fees cost so much over time?

faqs.a: Sometimes. Decades of data show most active funds underperform their index after fees. A higher fee can be justified only if the fund consistently beats the market by more than the fee - rare, and impossible to predict in advance.
faqs.q: Are expensive funds ever worth it?

faqs.a: Look for the expense ratio (TER) in the fund factsheet, plus entry/exit loads, platform charges, and adviser fees. In India, check whether you hold regular plans (higher fee, pays commission) vs direct plans (lower fee, same fund).
faqs.q: What fees should I look for?

faqs.a: Yes, dramatically. Switching a $10,000 investment from a 1.5% fee fund to a 0.2% fee fund at 7% return over 30 years keeps roughly an extra $20,000. Same market return, same risk - the only difference is who keeps the money.
faqs.q: Does switching to a cheaper fund really matter?

faqs.a: Advisers paid by commission may steer you to high-fee products. Ask directly: how are you paid, and what is the total annual cost of what you recommend? Fee-only advisers remove this conflict.

investment-fee-calculator.formula:
Future value, no fee = P x (1 + r)^t.
Future value, with fee = P x (1 + r - fee)^t.
Cost of fees = FV no fee - FV with fee.
Example: 10,000 x 1.07^30 = 76,122.55; 10,000 x 1.055^30 = 49,839.51; cost = 26,283.04.
howTo: Enter the expected gross annual return before fees.
Enter the fund's annual fee (expense ratio) as a percentage.
Enter the investment horizon in years.
Read how much the fee costs you in dollars and as a share of your final balance.
keyFacts: A 1% annual fee sounds tiny but compounds into a huge lifetime cost.
At 7% return over 30 years, a 1.5% fee eats about 35% of your final balance.
Index funds typically charge 0.03-0.20%; active funds often charge 0.75-2%.
Fees are charged every year on your whole balance, including past gains.
The fee drag grows with time: 10 years is mild, 30 years is brutal.
Net return is what matters - gross return minus all fees.
